payload.author: airborne12
payload.title: [fix](be) Decouple SNII BM25 scoring from CommonGrams

payload.author: github-actions
payload.body:
I found three blocking correctness/compatibility defects and one API-contract defect, so I am requesting changes.

Findings

- P1: nullable ARRAY rows can persist and count arbitrary nested payload beneath an outer SQL NULL, corrupting BM25 df/avgdl for surviving rows.
- P1: the metadata-free plain-T3 shape reuses format version 1 and is rejected by pre-PR readers during rolling operation.
- P1: the non-nullable ADD INDEX path drops all-empty ARRAY batches, shifting later postings and norms to the wrong row IDs.
- P3: the changed encoded_norm contract promises a normless fallback that the implementation does not provide.

Checkpoint conclusions

- Goal and scope: the scalar ordinary-analyzed scoring path is focused and works by inspection, but the goal is not safely achieved for ARRAY ingestion or mixed-version operation.
- User focus: no additional focus was provided; the complete diff was reviewed.
- Concurrency, lifecycle, and static initialization: writer ownership, norm-cache publication, streamed-session abort, and failure cleanup were traced; no additional lock-order, publication, or leak issue was found.
- Configuration and compatibility: no new dynamic config was introduced. The persisted T3 semantic change lacks a version/capability boundary, as reported inline. Mixed T2/T3 compaction itself fails native preflight and raw-rebuilds correctly.
- Parallel and special-case paths: scalar rows, scalar null runs, normal ARRAY rows, nested-null elements, analyzer failures, deletion remapping, and homogeneous plain-T3 compaction are coherent. Outer-null ARRAY and non-nullable ADD INDEX are the two broken sibling paths reported inline.
- Persistence/data correctness and FE/BE state: this is a BE-only persisted-index change; no FE variable or transaction path changed. Core/norm cardinality checks and row-id remapping are otherwise consistent, but the on-disk discriminator issue is blocking.
- Tests and current results: the new scalar/provider tests and existing native-vs-rebuild coverage are useful, but there is no production-path proof for the two ARRAY failures or a base-reader/new-writer compatibility test. Per the review runner instruction I did not build locally. Current PR checks show compile, BE UT, formatter, P0, coverage, cloud, and performance passing; NonConcurrent Regression is currently failing.
- Observability: existing status propagation identifies rejected shapes; no separate observability defect was found.
- Performance: the intended extra frequency regions and one norm byte per row are bounded and tracked/reserved on the inspected paths; the performance check passes.
- Other: the normless encoded_norm documentation mismatch is reported as P3.

Review completeness: two full rounds completed. In round 2, both normal reviewers and the separate risk-focused reviewer returned NO_NEW_VALUABLE_FINDINGS; every candidate is accepted, deduplicated, or dismissed with code evidence.

payload.author: github-actions
payload.body:
Review opinion: no new distinct correctness, lifecycle, compatibility, performance, or coverage issue was found at head `6ab16d07f22f49c8882f02f1f8e08c77500fe044`, so this pass adds no inline comments. The existing four review threads and author replies were treated as strict duplicate fences; this comment does not supersede their live review state.

Checkpoint conclusions

- Goal and proof: The change decouples BM25 scoring for ordinary analyzed, position-enabled SNII indexes from CommonGrams. The writer emits frequencies and one norm per logical row, the reader/provider admit only validated metadata-free scoring T3, collection statistics use raw-key physical statistics for plain segments and semantic/escaped statistics for CommonGrams, and native compaction preserves the same shape. Production-path unit tests, whole-image goldens, mixed-segment tests, and pre/post-compaction regression coverage substantiate that chain.
- Focus and scope: No additional user focus was provided. The implementation is focused on the writer/reader/statistics/compaction contracts plus the two ARRAY producers and their tests; it reuses the existing streamed writer, statistics provider, and collection-scoring machinery.
- Concurrency, lifecycle, and statics: The changed ingestion and compaction work is synchronous and segment/session-local. No new thread entry, shared mutable state, lock ordering, cross-TU static initialization, or reference cycle is introduced. The existing norms-cache publication protocol is unchanged, and streamed sessions remain one-shot, poison-on-error, and aborted together on failure.
- Error handling and memory safety: Reviewed `Status` values propagate through the changed producers, readers, eligibility checks, streamed sessions, and finalization. Malformed configs, missing/invalid norms, bad statistics, corrupt postings, and incomplete row-id mappings fail closed. Norms, NULL vectors, source frames, posting workspaces, and auxiliary writer sections remain covered by `MemoryReporter` reservation/ownership, with release or abort on all inspected failure paths.
- Data correctness and BE NULL handling: Scalar, nullable scalar, ARRAY, empty ARRAY, nested-NULL, outer-NULL, direct-write, and ADD INDEX paths now advance exactly one docid and one norm per logical row. Outer-NULL payload is suppressed while retaining a zero norm and NULL docid. Plain/CommonGrams mixtures retain per-segment key routing and consistent N/avgdl/df semantics; native compaction remaps postings, deletes, NULLs, and norms through the validated conversion and reconstructs live term statistics.
- Configuration and compatibility: No configuration item or FE/BE variable is added. The existing CommonGrams build toggle is revalidated at compaction preflight and execution, and heterogeneous shapes safely fall back or fail before publication. The metadata-free-T3 rolling/readback question, including compacted rowsets, is exactly the already-live compatibility thread and was not duplicated; no distinct format issue survived review.
- Parallel paths and conditions: The new nullable-ARRAY virtual preserves the old values-then-null-map contract for CLucene and SNII BKD, while SNII text provides the combined override and ANN remains on its fixed-dimension path. Plain T2, plain T3, CommonGrams T3, missing-scoring-component, mixed-segment, multi-destination, deletion, corruption, and abort paths were traced. The surviving numeric all-empty ARRAY guard is the same producer/mechanism already covered by the live all-empty ARRAY thread and explicit author reply.
- Tests and results: Test intent and expected results are consistent by inspection: analyzed whole-image hashes change, the keyword hash remains stable, readback asserts exact config/stats/norm behavior, ARRAY fixes use production producers, and the existing native-vs-raw integration test now selects plain T3 across two logical indexes and two destination segments and byte-compares complete outputs. payload.author: airborne12
payload.body:
Updated: the `inverted_index_p0.storage_format.test_common_grams_snii` regression case would have failed on the previous revision. Two of its assertions expected `SNII semantic scoring metadata is missing`, and the change makes both of those queries succeed — but one of them only after fixing a real bug in the patch.

**A defect the regression case exposed.** The plain shape was signalled by an EMPTY base-analyzer fingerprint, because only a CommonGrams segment records one (its term keys depend on the dictionary identity). That empty value then flowed into the cross-segment check "were these two segments analyzed with the same analyzer", where `"" != "cg_default_analyzer-fingerprint"` read as *a different analyzer* and rejected the whole collection. A table holding one CommonGrams segment and one plain segment for the same field — what you get by toggling `enable_common_grams_index_build` between loads — was refused with a message that was not merely unhelpful but false: both segments were analyzed by the same analyzer, one simply did not build grams.

Their statistics are combinable, and that is the point of the semantic counts existing at all:

```
CommonGrams segment  'alpha beta the world'   physical sum_total_term_freq = 6  (4 tokens + 2 grams)
                                              metadata.scoring_token_count = 4   <- used
plain segment        'alpha beta the worker'  physical sum_total_term_freq = 4   <- used, already semantic
                                              collection: N = 2, tokens = 8, avgdl = 4
```

Summing the physical values would give avgdl 5. Document frequency is comparable too: `SpimiTermBuffer::add_common_gram_and_plain` writes the gram AND the token's own plain posting, so plain postings are complete in a CommonGrams segment and df is measured identically on both sides.

Fixed by requiring BOTH fingerprints to be present before comparing them, and by never letting an absent identity overwrite a recorded one.

**Test changes:**

- New `CollectionStatisticsTest.SniiMixedCommonGramsAndPlainSegmentsCombine` drives `CollectionStatistics::collect` over one segment of each shape and asserts the summed statistics.
- `LegacyAndCommonGramsMixRejectsWholeCollection` went red and was retargeted rather than deleted. Its intent — a segment with no scoring data poisons a collection it is mixed into — is still right; only its marker was stale. It faked "no CommonGrams metadata but T3 with norms", a shape that could not exist while scoring rode on CommonGrams and is now the ordinary analyzed segment. It now uses the real marker, absent norms.
- The two regression assertions expect the ranking to match the V3 control (`assertEquals(rankedIds(...))`) instead of an exception. No new `qt_` outputs were added, so no `.out` file needs regenerating.

Full inverted-index suites: 3213 tests, 0 failures. clang-format 16 clean; clang-tidy reports nothing on any added line.

payload.author: Mryange
payload.title: [feature](function) Add array_except_all scalar function

payload.author: github-actions
payload.body:
Request changes: the core loop implements saturating multiset subtraction in left-input order, and the registration/include wiring is coherent, but five distinct issues remain.

Goal and scope: the PR is focused on `array_except_all`; the generic supported-type path, per-row count reset, NULL multiplicity, result offsets, and string-key lifetime are otherwise sound.

Correctness and compatibility: FE admits `ARRAY<VARBINARY>` even though BE cannot dispatch it, and FLOAT/DOUBLE NaNs use equality semantics inconsistent with Doris. There is no storage-format, protocol, rolling-upgrade, transaction, persistence, or data-write change.

Concurrency, lifecycle, and configuration: the implementation is function-local and introduces no shared mutable state, special lifecycle, or new configuration. The existing constant-fold control exposes the all-constant execution path described inline.

Parallel/special paths: FE registration, scalar visitor fallback, BE factory registration, default outer-NULL handling, common-type coercion, one-constant execution, source discovery, and unity/direct-include hygiene were traced. The both-constant path unnecessarily bypasses expression/framework caching and expands the result once per block row.

Performance and memory: the user-proportional count map bypasses Doris query-memory accounting, and the all-constant override can multiply CPU and result memory by the block row count.

Tests and results: the added expected values cover duplicates, NULLs, row reset, constants, coercion, and several scalar families, but they do not prove unsorted left-order preservation, NaN cancellation, the VARBINARY boundary, or multi-row all-constant result shape. No build or test binary was run because the review bundle prohibits builds; the repository's pure-text build-hygiene check passed.

Observability: no additional logging or metrics are required once the execution failures and resource-accounting defects are fixed. User focus: no additional focus point was supplied.

Review completion: three independent review rounds converged with no new finding in the final round. All surviving candidates are represented by the four inline comments below (the two line-40 defects share one anchor).

payload.body: ## Pull request overview > [!WARNING] > Copilot couldn't run its full agentic review because it didn't start before the timeout. Make sure your repository has a runner available, or add a `copilot-code-review.yml` file specifying one with the `runs-on` attribute. See the [docs](https://gh.io/AA11tgch) for more details. Removes a redundant cloud partition version fetch during SQL cache validation to avoid an unnecessary Meta Service RPC. **Changes:** - Removed the batch version fetch call (`getVersionInBatchForCloudMode`) during table/partition validation. - Removed the associated `RpcException` handling path for that call. - Cleaned up an unused `Collection` import. --- 💡 Add a `code-review` agent skill or configure MCP servers for context-aware, tailored reviews. payload.author: github-actions
payload.body:
Review complete: I found no new non-duplicate blocking issue in this change.

Critical checkpoint conclusions:
- Goal and correctness: The deletion accomplishes the stated goal. At cache creation, Doris still records the OLAP table version and the partition-derived BE cache gate. At lookup, freshness is decided by the stored-versus-current table version plus explicit existence checks for every scanned partition. The removed cloud batch call refreshed partition-object caches, but its returned versions were never compared or passed to the FE/BE cache consumer. Non-cloud behavior is unchanged because that helper was a no-op there.
- Scope and reuse: The PR is a focused one-file deletion. The creation-time batch fetch remains in `CacheAnalyzer`, where its partition versions and timestamps are actually consumed. Import cleanup is correct; the remaining `RpcException` import is still needed by the table-version check.
- Concurrency and lifecycle: No shared state, ownership, or lock order is added. The lookup path already holds statement table read locks, so removing the possible Meta Service partition RPC shortens work under those locks. Cloud commit, peer-FE propagation, and periodic sync paths continue to maintain table-version freshness.
- Errors and observability: Table-version RPC failures still log and invalidate the SQL-cache entry, and the outer lookup boundary still invalidates on unexpected failures. The removed partition-RPC failure behavior is already covered by the existing Copilot thread, so I did not duplicate it.
- Configuration and compatibility: No configuration, persistence, protocol, storage-format, FE-BE variable, or rolling-upgrade contract changes are introduced. Cloud/non-cloud branches and the parallel creation-versus-validation paths remain consistent.
- Performance: The change removes sorting/list construction, version-cache locking, and a possible Meta Service batch RPC whose result was unused. `ScanTable.getScanPartitions()` is now called once and is a direct Lombok field getter.
- Tests: Existing SQL-cache regression coverage exercises invalidation after inserts, insert overwrite, add/drop/replace partition, and truncation, including cloud-specific behavior. This PR adds no dedicated no-RPC call-count test, and this review did not run builds or tests per the runner instructions. The live FE CheckStyle, title, license, formatter, secret, and large-file checks are green.
- User focus: No additional user-provided focus was specified.

Overall, the change is small, coherent, and safe based on the traced creation-to-lookup and cloud version-publication flows. Review status: complete, with zero new inline comments after duplicate fencing against both existing review threads.

payload.body:
Automated review result: request changes

I found two blocking issues: FE and BE still disagree on locale-dependent keyword normalization, leaving an FE-accepted two-argument call on the BE crash path; and the added BE unit test fails before it can prove the fix, then still uses a row shape that cannot independently exercise the cases.

Critical checkpoint conclusions:

- Goal and proof: the BE change handles locale-independent ASCII case variants, but does not fully align with FE accepted-input semantics; the new test does not currently provide valid proof.
- Scope/focus: the production diff is compact and focused. Fixing FE normalization and restructuring the test are both required to complete the stated goal.
- Concurrency: the function is stateless and uses block-local data; no shared-state, lock-order, or atomic concern applies.
- Lifecycle/static initialization: no lifecycle, ownership-cycle, destructor, or cross-TU static initialization change is introduced.
- Configuration: no configuration item or dynamic-reload behavior is added.
- Compatibility: no symbol, protocol, storage-format, or persisted-data change is present. Exact comparisons preserve locale-independent FE-valid tokens and reject existing invalid prefixes; locale parity remains the compatibility gap.

Request changes: the proposed retryable cleanup still has four resource-lifecycle regressions.

Critical checkpoints:
- Retry correctness and ownership: a failed Paimon writer is retained after its shared spill IOManager has been closed and its directories deleted, so later cleanup may never recover.
- Abort/artifact cleanup: the all-failure no-prepare abort path loses already-flushed append/postpone file metadata and relies on a manual orphan-cleanup job that Doris does not run.
- JNI lifecycle: the writer global reference, defining-class/method-ID lifetime, cross-thread JNIEnv acquisition, and native-manager release order are otherwise sound, but persistent retries leak exception-local JNI strings.
- Arrow C Data: Arrow 19 allocator close is terminal-on-throw; a second no-op close can be mistaken for cleanup after a partial import retained foreign buffers.
- Concurrency/authentication: mutex serialization, bounded in-flight admission, and retained authenticator behavior produced no additional issue.
- Compatibility/configuration/performance: no separate regression found.
- Tests: the new retryable lambda does not exercise real Paimon dependency ordering, real RootAllocator behavior, abort artifacts, or native quarantine repetition.
- Release note: the intended recovery behavior is not yet achieved because the accepted retry paths can remain broken or falsely report success.

payload.author: Gabriel39
payload.body:
Thanks for working on making Paimon JNI cleanup recoverable after OOM. I found four lifecycle issues that need to be addressed before this recovery path is safe:

1. Do not close the spill IOManager while the writer close is still unconfirmed (PaimonJniWriter.java:585-607). closeWriter() retains writer after writer.close() fails, but still closes ioManager. Paimon 1.4.2 closes its FileChannelManager by deleting the spill directories, so the retained writer can lose resources needed by its remaining flush/compaction tasks. A later retry may then fail permanently and keep Paimon writes fenced. Please retain the IOManager together with the writer and close it only after the writer has closed successfully.

2. The new abort path can leave already-flushed files orphaned (PaimonJniWriter.java:671-691). On a write failure, preparedCommitMessages is normally empty, but append/postpone writers may already have flushed data files. In Paimon 1.4.2 those files are surfaced through prepareCommit; close alone does not delete all of them. Doris does not schedule remove_orphan_files, so relying on Paimon orphan cleanup can leak files indefinitely. Please preserve enough state to retry an explicit cleanup, or add a cleanup path that does not require a high-memory prepareCommit.

3. RootAllocator.close() is not retryable in the way closeResources() assumes (PaimonJniWriter.java:531-549). Arrow 19.0.0 BaseAllocator sets isClosed before checking for outstanding buffers. If the first close throws, the second call returns immediately; this code then clears allocator and reports cleanup success even though imported C Data buffers may remain outstanding. Please track and close the imported resources themselves, and do not use a second allocator.close() return as proof that cleanup completed.

4. Repeated native retries leak JNI local references (jni_paimon_write_backend.cpp:56-65). Each failed retry calls GetJniExceptionMsg with stack logging. That helper deletes the throwable but not the generated message and stack-trace jstrings. These calls run on long-lived attached BE threads without a local JNI frame, so repeated failures accumulate local refs and can trigger another OOM/local-reference-table exhaustion. Please delete those local refs or wrap each retry in PushLocalFrame/PopLocalFrame.

The compile and regular UT/regression checks pass, but BE changed-line coverage is 0/82 and the Arrow/Paimon lifecycle test is skipped, so these failure paths are currently untested.

payload.author: zyp-V
payload.title: [improvement](be) Separate local tablet schemas from metadata

payload.author: github-actions
payload.body:
Requesting changes: the schema-separation migration is not safe across publication, restart, downgrade, clone failure, cleanup, and index-rewrite paths. I found 12 substantiated issues, detailed inline.

Review status: capped/incomplete. Two new valuable findings survived the third and maximum independent round, so this review includes every validated issue but does not claim convergence.

Critical checkpoint conclusions:
- Goal and proof: the happy path reduces inline metadata, but the implementation does not preserve the exact-schema, recoverability, or lifecycle invariants needed to prove the change safe.
- Scope and focus: all 27 authoritative changed files were reviewed. No additional user focus was supplied. The unrelated JSON whitespace edit is out of scope and the live Clang Formatter check is failing on it.
- Concurrency and locks: a writer-publication race can create a stripped rowset without its schema key; index add/drop performs O(rowsets) synchronous metadata reads while holding the exclusive header lock. No separate lock-order deadlock was found.
- Lifecycle and errors: force restore, direct administrative deletion, and shutdown cleanup each mishandle UID-scoped schema ownership or broken-header cleanup; clone can mutate live ownership before a fallible schema write.
- Configuration: no new configuration defect was found. Existing default startup behavior makes a retained broken header fatal.
- Compatibility and protocol: the first migrated checkpoint is unreadable by the immediately prior BE; normal snapshot, clone-header, storage-migration, cloud, and tool transfer boundaries otherwise remain self-contained.
- Parallel paths and conditions: normal writers, the direct PushHandler writer, standalone recovery, CCR and row-binlog export, index add/drop, incremental/full clone, force restore, normal drop, administrative delete, and path-present/path-absent shutdown cleanup were traced.
- Tests and results: no build or test was run because the review bundle forbids it. The read-only BE build-hygiene check passed. The live Clang Formatter check fails. One changed path-GC test aborts during setup, and crash/restart/concurrency/downgrade/index/restore/delete/malformed-schema coverage is missing.
- Observability: dependency lookup failures are mislabeled as protobuf parse failures or conflated with header absence, so current logs/status propagation are insufficient.
- Transaction, persistence, and crash safety: schema publication is not guaranteed before stripped rowset metadata; upgrade recovery can later strip the only inline historical schema; clone failure can leave live rowsets pointing to files the caller unlinks.
- Data-write atomicity: successful schema-before-meta writes are directionally safe, but the writer flag, one-time migration flag, version-only identity, and post-mutation clone write create broken-reference windows.
- Transmitted variables and memory/static initialization: no new FE/BE transmitted-variable, static-initialization, or nullable-memory issue was found.
- Performance: repeated RocksDB reads under the exclusive header lock are a regression proportional to rowset count rather than distinct schemas.

payload.title: branch-4.1:[improvement](be) Make Iceberg data file writes synchronous

payload.author: github-actions
payload.body:
Request changes.

I found two blocking correctness defects and one behavioral-coverage gap in the synchronous Iceberg sink conversion:

- The spill local state destroys its owning writer while workload-group accounting can still be between an unsynchronized null check and `current_writer()`, creating a teardown use-after-free.
- A cancellation arriving during the final task execution can leave the scheduler-local status OK; both new closes then finalize and record files as success instead of deleting the cancelled query's objects.
- The added test checks only inheritance/blockability/dependency shape and never drives the converted init/open/write/EOS/close behavior.

Critical checkpoints: blocking-scheduler routing, direct write-error propagation, normal empty/non-empty EOS admission, close-status precedence, expression-vector ownership, all `VIcebergTableWriter` callers, MERGE prepared-block layout/deferred cleanup, explicit async-template removal, and ordinary/spill file cleanup were traced. Apart from the reported cancellation path, those mechanisms remain coherent. The expression vectors outlive every writer use, and the MERGE caller remains aligned. A live inline comment already covers EOS spill-finalization reservation, so I did not duplicate it. There was no additional user-provided review focus.

The authoritative nine-file diff completed three review rounds and converged with no unresolved candidates. The PR is still open at the reviewed head/base. Per the runner instructions I did not run a local build; live COMPILE and BE UT checks are still pending, while style, formatter, license, and dependency checks have passed. The repository-local code-review `SKILL.md` was not present in this checkout, so I followed the complete bundle review contract directly.

payload.author: github-actions
payload.body:
Requesting changes for three independently reproduced memory-admission defects in the spill-enabled sorted Iceberg write path.

Critical checkpoints

- Correctness and memory: the EOS estimate is not an upper bound on merger allocation, cannot see writers created by the pending block, and uses a first-block-only row-width sample that does not preserve the configured spill byte bound.
- Lifecycle and cleanup: synchronous normal/spill init, open, write, EOS, terminal close, cancellation/error precedence, and deferred file cleanup were traced across success and failure paths; the current head addresses the previously reported lifecycle concerns.
- Concurrency and ownership: parent reset, atomic child snapshots, sorter locking, concurrent accounting/revoke, and delayed spill interleavings were checked; no distinct UAF, race, deadlock, or post-close spill issue remains.
- Compatibility: removal of the AsyncResultWriter base, all constructor/template call sites, blocking scheduler classification, expression/profile lifetimes, and the still-async MERGE embedding were checked without finding a separate compatibility issue.
- Tests: the new lifecycle and arithmetic tests cover the fixed status/ownership paths, but they do not construct the real intermediate merger, exercise pending-block/new-partition admission, or spill a narrow-first/wide-later sequence; those gaps are incorporated into the three inline findings.
- Existing threads: the four prior inline concerns and their fix replies were treated as a hard duplicate fence; these three findings are distinct post-fix amount and width-skew defects.
- User focus: no additional user-provided review focus was supplied; the full PR was reviewed.
- CI at review time: style, formatter, license, dependency review, and other reported lightweight gates pass; BE UT and COMPILE are still pending.

Review completion: two rounds completed. In Round 2, both independent whole-PR reviewers and the separate risk-focused reviewer returned NO_NEW_VALUABLE_FINDINGS while reproducing the same three accepted issues. Every candidate is adjudicated and the review converged.

The existing assertions still prove that a missing-binding response raises the expected Nereids `AnalysisException`, installs no wrapper state, can be retried successfully, and issues two complete requests.

- Compatibility, configuration, persistence, writes, and FE-BE propagation: no configuration definition, protocol/storage format, journal, transaction, data-write path, or FE-BE variable changes are present.

Live Checkstyle passed. payload.title: [improvement](be) Avoid temporary strings in float serialization

payload.author: github-actions
payload.body:
Review conclusion: no blocking issues found. This is a focused, behavior-preserving allocation optimization, so this review intentionally has no inline comments.

Critical checkpoint conclusions:

- Goal and correctness: achieved. FLOAT/DOUBLE JSON serialization now avoids the intermediate `std::string`; both old and new paths call the same `_fast_to_buffer`, use the same returned length, and exclude the same trailing NUL.
- Scope and clarity: the PR changes only the FLOAT/DOUBLE branch of `DataTypeNumberSerDe<T>::serialize_one_cell_to_json`; the one-line replacement is small and reuses the established direct-writer helper.
- Concurrency and lifecycle: no shared state, locks, threads, static initialization, ownership handoff, or special cleanup is introduced. Formatting uses a local value and stack buffer, then synchronously copies into the caller-owned writer.
- Buffer and error safety: exact `float`/`double` overloads are selected; fixed buffers retain the existing bounds; `BufferWritable::write` performs the same copy and offset increment as before. The `Status` contract is unchanged; the eliminated temporary can no longer allocate or fail independently, while any buffer-growth failure still occurs in `BufferWritable::write` before `_now_offset` advances.
- Compatibility and parallel paths: serialized bytes remain governed by the same formatter for finite values, signed zero, NaN, and both infinities. Request changes. The one-runnable-per-`ScannerContext` design is focused and its marker/task-ownership protocol is mostly balanced, but the three inline comments cover four defects: missing shared-LIMIT and fatal-status admission gates at one predicate, low-memory scheduler drift, and lost scanner wait-time attribution.

Critical checkpoint conclusions:

- Goal and proof: Bounding ThreadPool queue entries per Context is achieved structurally, but the accepted admission, parity, and observability regressions mean the runtime goal is not yet correctly preserved. The added tests prove ordinary/adaptive admission, rejection, caught admission failure, and terminal EOS, not the reported interleavings.
- Scope and clarity: The six-file BE scan-scheduler change is focused. The main clarity risk is duplicated admission policy between ThreadPool and TaskExecutor, which caused the shared-LIMIT and low-memory divergences.
- Concurrency and locking: Pipeline/operator threads, scanner workers, and queued Context callbacks synchronize marker state, pending/completed queues, terminal publication, and combined occupancy with `_transfer_lock`; scanning remains outside it. ThreadPool releases its own lock before callbacks, and no reverse lock edge, deadlock, duplicate task transition, or lost dependency wake survived review. The missing terminal gates nevertheless allow stale callbacks to race with LIMIT or error publication.
- Lifecycle and static initialization: Callback-held `shared_ptr` ownership, `TaskExecutionContext` expiry, retained-runnable create failure, WorkloadGroup teardown, and pool shutdown were traced and remain safe; active callbacks are drained and no cycle or cross-TU static-initialization issue applies.
- Error handling and data correctness: Status/exception paths are generally surfaced, but a stale callback can replace the original scan/schema error with `TOO_MANY_TASKS`, and shared-LIMIT completion can be converted from success to failure. These are covered by the P1 comment.
- Memory safety and ownership: Completed-block ownership, in-flight decrement, cached-block accounting, and success/EOS/error/cancellation handoffs remain balanced. No separate allocation, nullable-column, or memory-safety defect applies.
- Configuration and compatibility: No configuration, ABI, protocol, storage-format, rolling-upgrade, or FE-BE variable change is introduced.
- Parallel paths and special conditions: TaskExecutor is the relevant parallel path. Its progress-aware shared-LIMIT gate and running-scanner low-memory cap are not preserved by the ThreadPool predicate; the necessary asymmetric conditions are described inline.
- Tests and results: The PR reports 35 `ScannerContextTest` and 18 `ThreadPoolTest` cases plus format and build-hygiene checks. This review harness forbids rerunning builds/tests; current CI exposes successful formatter/style/security checks but no BE build/UT result. Deterministic stale-callback, low-memory completed/pending/in-flight parity, and delayed-worker profile tests are still needed. No regression `.out` result is involved.
- Observability and performance: `ScannerWorkerWaitTime` now omits Context queue residence, and low-memory mode can suppress all active scanning behind four completed blocks. Both regressions are called out inline; the queue-bounding objective is otherwise a reasonable performance improvement.

payload.author: github-actions
payload.body:
Request changes. This review is capped/incomplete after the maximum three delegated rounds: rounds 1 and 2 found accepted issues, and round 3 still found two new accepted issues, so I am not claiming convergence. The twelve blocking findings are attached inline.

Critical checkpoint conclusions:
- Goal/proof: the PR narrows the earlier refactor and enables TaskExecutor by default, but it does not do so safely; the changed tests do not prove submission ownership, shutdown/resize liveness, LIMIT behavior, or TaskExecutor resource governance.
- Scope/focus: all nine changed files and their production callers were reviewed. The diff is small, but the default switch exposes pre-existing TimeSharing failure paths while the ThreadPool rollback reintroduces defects covered by three deleted regressions.
- Concurrency/thread safety: submitters, worker creators, dispatch workers, shutdown, and WorkloadGroup resize threads share live/pending counts and queues under their pool locks. Moving thread creation outside the lock is reasonable, but publication/rollback, condition-variable notification, and retirement ordering are incorrect in both pool implementations. Scanner `_transfer_lock` ordering and retained Context lifetime were otherwise verified.
- Error handling: generic ThreadPool can return non-OK after retaining work; TimeSharing ignores initial submit errors; the fallback scanner path turns recoverable capacity pressure terminal; and the new LIMIT re-enqueue path can surface `TOO_MANY_TASKS` after the result is complete. These violate the error-means-failure contract.
- Lifecycle: runnable/split ownership, in-flight slots, dependencies, worker replacement, and stop/wait were traced end to end. MAIN-1 through MAIN-3, MAIN-5, MAIN-9, and MAIN-10 are lifecycle/liveness failures. No new static-initialization or ownership-cycle issue was found.
- Configuration: no new item is added, but two startup defaults change. Enabling TaskExecutor is unsafe until its submit, low-memory, shutdown, resize, and per-task-cap contracts are fixed. The production constructor currently makes the documented per-task maximum ineffective.
- Parallel paths/special conditions: generic ThreadPool and TimeSharing contain independent sibling failures, and both scanner schedulers were reviewed. The terminal-before-resubmit check is sound only for the zero-progress state covered by the new test; the shared-LIMIT checks miss admitted pre-open work and `current_scan_task`.
- Tests/results: no local build or test was run because this was a review-only task. The author reports 34/34 scanner and 18/18 ThreadPool ASAN tests passing, but the PR deletes exact regressions for failed first-worker publication, shrink-with-failed-replacement, and zero maximum, and lacks deterministic TaskExecutor saturation/creation/stop/resize/low-memory/per-task-cap/LIMIT coverage. No result files changed.
- Observability: removing the Context queue timer reduces per-query visibility, but pool-wide metrics/logging remain and this was dismissed as an explicit scope tradeoff rather than a blocker. Silent TaskExecutor submit failure is a correctness issue, not merely observability.
- Compatibility/data correctness: no protocol, storage-format, rolling-upgrade, transaction, persistence, data-write, FE-BE variable, or nullable-column path changes apply. Shared-LIMIT result correctness is affected by MAIN-7 and MAIN-12.

payload.title: [fix](audit) preserve final statistics for external writes

payload.author: github-actions
payload.body:
Request changes: the idle, unique-ID happy path is notified, but this change does not reliably publish truly final DML statistics before FE's audit deadline and introduces material lifecycle, concurrency, and reporting-cadence hazards.

Six inline comments cover seven validated issues: QueryContext destruction is neither a timely nor a final all-producer completion boundary; a slow FE blocks healthy-FE completion reporting; same-ID group-commit generations can replace or erase one another; finished state is published before its timestamp; sustained completions can drive continuous full-map reporting; and the added test does not execute the production integration.

Critical checkpoint conclusions:
- Goal and tests: the general deadline/finality goal is not met. Runtime-filter retention can delay the trigger, a blocked FE can delay the only consumer beyond 5 seconds, and ResourceContext-only producers can mutate the peak after a successful final report. The test proves only the notification bit.
- Scope and design: the textual diff is focused, but destructor timing plus the existing global synchronous reporter is not the explicit all-producers-complete, bounded reporting path the goal requires.
- Concurrency and locks: the new mutex/CV predicate, timeout reset, and shutdown wake are sound; no lost wake, nested-lock deadlock, or manager UAF was found. The unsafe concurrency is in generation-blind map snapshot/RPC/erase, two-field finish publication, and post-QueryContext ResourceContext producers.
- Lifecycle and initialization: daemon/ExecEnv teardown order is safe and no ownership cycle or cross-TU static-initialization issue was added. Runtime-filter ownership delays QueryContext destruction, while LoadChannel/LoadStream ownership can outlive it.
- Configuration and compatibility: no config, Thrift field, storage format, symbol contract, EditLog, or rolling-upgrade protocol changed. The existing 60-second BE RPC timeout versus FE's 5-second audit wait is material.
- Parallel and conditional paths: LOAD classification is appropriate, but runtime-filter INSERT SELECT, same-ID group commit, legacy LoadChannel, and newer LoadStream expose the issues above; SELECT/EXTERNAL behavior is otherwise unchanged.

payload.author: HappenLee
payload.body:
I found two remaining issues in the current head (`dc20751b200547b32f9a9b1ec0f8beab68463dd9`):

### [P1] `map_from_arrays(map_keys(m), map_values(m))` can still lose precision

`MapFromArrays.computePrecision()` preserves the two array element types only after its arguments have been resolved. However, `MapKeys` and `MapValues` do not implement `ComputePrecision`, so their generic precision coercion can first cast both sides of the source MAP to a common type.

For example, for:

```sql
m = map(
    cast(1 as decimalv3(38, 0)),
    cast(0.12345678901234567890123456789012345678 as decimalv3(38, 38)))

map_from_arrays(map_keys(m), map_values(m))
```

the analyzed result is currently:

```text
MAP<DECIMALV3(38,6), DECIMALV3(38,6)>
```

instead of:

```text
MAP<DECIMALV3(38,0), DECIMALV3(38,38)>
```

The analyzed expression tree contains a cast from `MAP<DECIMALV3(38,0),DECIMALV3(38,38)>` to `MAP<DECIMALV3(38,6),DECIMALV3(38,6)>`, so the value can lose 32 fractional digits before reaching `map_from_arrays`.

The existing inverse regression test only uses `MAP<INT,INT>`, while the precision tests pass arrays directly to `map_from_arrays`, so this path is not covered.

Suggested minimal fix: make `MapKeys` and `MapValues` implement `ComputePrecision` and return the resolved signature unchanged, as this PR already does for `MapEntries`. Please also add DECIMALV3 and DATETIMEV2 inverse tests using `map_from_arrays(map_keys(m), map_values(m))`.

### [P3] Extra blank line at EOF

`git diff --check` reports:

```text
regression-test/data/query_p0/sql_functions/map_functions/test_map_from_arrays_entries.out:41: new blank line at EOF.
```

Please remove the extra final blank line from the generated result file.

payload.author: github-actions
payload.body:
## Review conclusion

Request changes. The NULL-aware copy is correct once CHAR cloning is entered, but the unchanged aggregate padding predicate can still bypass that clone. MAIN-001 gives a concrete mixed nullable batch that fails in debug and can abort short-key encoding or write/index an undersized live CHAR value in release.

The review converged after two rounds: the Round 2 normal full review and adversarial risk recheck both returned `NO_NEW_VALUABLE_FINDINGS`, and every candidate is accepted, merged, or dismissed with code evidence.

## Critical checkpoint conclusions

- **Goal and test proof:** Not fully achieved. Hidden NULL payloads are skipped only after `should_padding()` chooses to clone, and no production CHAR-converter test exercises the new null-map branch or the aggregate-cancellation case.
- **Scope and reuse:** The two-file change is small and localized, and it reuses the existing converter; the padding predicate must participate in the same null-aware policy for the fix to be complete.
- **Concurrency and lifecycle:** No new shared state, locking, thread entry, or static initialization is introduced. The origin null map is correctly aligned with whole-column cloning across direct, partial, STRUCT, ARRAY, and MAP paths; `_typed_column` and `_column` keep source and cloned storage alive through synchronous writer consumption.
- **Configuration, compatibility, and FE-BE propagation:** No configuration, protocol, symbol contract, FE-BE variable, rolling-upgrade, or intended storage-format change is introduced.
- **Parallel paths and special conditions:** SegmentWriter and VerticalSegmentWriter share this converter, and nested CHAR children use the same helper. The new NULL condition itself is valid, but its entry guard remains null-unaware as described inline.
- **Error and data-write correctness:** The bypass trips only a `DCHECK` in debug; in release an undersized live `Slice` reaches page/index writers, and CHAR short-key encoding has an unconditional width `CHECK`. This is the blocking correctness issue. No transaction, delete-bitmap, EditLog, visibility-version, or failover state is otherwise changed.
- **Testing and results:** No test file changed. Existing helper tests use non-null inputs and do not execute this branch. Per the review-runner contract, no builds or tests were run during this review.
- **Performance, memory, and observability:** No material allocation-accounting or observability regression was found. A null-aware scan can retain the current aggregate fast path for non-nullable input and inspect only live rows for nullable input.
- **Additional issues and user focus:** No other substantiated issue remains, and no additional user-provided focus was specified.

payload.author: github-actions

Review opinion: looks good; I found no blocking correctness issue and no inline finding to submit.

Critical checkpoint conclusions:

- Goal and proof: The reader now resolves `SpillReadDeserializeBlockTime` through the same canonical constant used by `SpillReadCounters::init`, so the existing profile counter is updated instead of a misspelled lookup returning null. `ReadDeserializeTimerIsRecorded` starts from a fresh zero-valued canonical counter, performs a real spill read, requires it to become positive, and confirms the old misspelled name is absent; it would fail with the old lookup.
- Scope and clarity: The production change is confined to counter lookup. The three fixture changes reuse the production counter initializers, preserve all reader/writer-required extras, and correct the former timer/byte unit mismatches without changing runtime data behavior.
- Concurrency: No execution scheduling or shared-state protocol changes. RuntimeProfile map access remains locked, counter values remain atomic, and every reader is constructed only after its owning local state has initialized the profile counters.
- Lifecycle: No ownership or release behavior changes. The stack-local `SpillWriteCounters`/`SpillReadCounters` holders in tests only retain aliases; RuntimeProfile owns the counters for the fixture lifetime.
- Configuration and compatibility: No configuration, FE-BE field, symbol, storage-format, transaction, persistence, or rolling-upgrade change. The externally visible counter name is unchanged.
- Parallel paths and conditions: All production SpillFileReader construction paths were traced, including spill sort, aggregation, hash join, repartitioning, multi-cast, and Iceberg sorted spill; each receives the canonical read-counter set with matching TIME_NS/UNIT/BYTES types before construction. The new DCHECKs express that registration invariant.
- Tests and results: The added BE unit test directly covers the regression, and the shared fixture setup prevents future test/production name drift. The exact PR head currently has passing COMPILE and BE UT checks; no local build was run in this review-only runner.
- Observability: This directly restores the existing deserialize-time signal and does not add or rename a metric. Existing sibling spill counters and identifiers remain unchanged.
- Performance and memory: Counter resolution remains constructor-only; the read hot path and allocation behavior are unchanged.
- Additional/user focus: No additional user focus was provided. The full changed-file sweep and round-1 full/risk reviews found no further valuable issue.

Review completeness: complete after one round; both normal full-review agents and the separate risk-focused agent returned `NO_NEW_VALUABLE_FINDINGS`, and the main-agent reconciliation left no unresolved candidate.

@zhangstar333 Thanks for running it. I can't read the failure myself — the TeamCity instance asks for a login — so could you paste the assertion block from the log? The part I need is:

```
Check tag '...' failed, line N, ... mismatch.
Expect cell is: ...
But real is   : ...
```

The tag name alone would probably be enough to pin it down.

For context on where I'd expect trouble: that suite covers three tables, and only the Float16 one records values that are not exactly representable.

- `f64_l2` / `f64_l2_flat` record the closed-form L2 ladder `0, 16, 64, 144, 256`
- `u8_hamming` / `u8_hamming_flat` record the hamming ladder `0, 1, 2, 3, 4`

Both are exact integers on any platform. The Float16 blocks are different — they record float32 cosine distances printed to 7-8 significant digits (`1.1920929E-7`, `0.2166698`, `0.29892504`, ...), computed from Float16 inputs.

I regenerated the goldens on macOS/arm64 after rebuilding the fixture. If the failing tag is `f16_cosine` or `f16_cosine_flat`, the likely cause is simply that those last digits come out differently on the CI's x86_64 build. In that case pinning them is the bug, not the values: that table uses directional data with no closed-form expected distance, so the distance column records whatever the platform computed rather than anything checkable — the row order is the part that carries meaning. The fix would be to keep the exact ladders for Float64 and UInt8 and drop `_distance` from the Float16 blocks, keeping the "self-distance is not exactly zero" observation as a tolerance-based assertion instead of a pinned literal.

If it is a different tag, that guess is wrong and I will dig into it from the log.

payload.author: FANNG1
payload.body:
Thanks — that log made it clear, and the guest login works, so I can read TeamCity myself from now on.

The cause is narrower than the digit drift I guessed at. Cosine distance is `1 - cos_sim`, and the cosine of a row against itself is mathematically exactly 1, so the distance is 0. It does not come out that way for `float16`: the query literal is the value *before* half-precision rounding while the column stores the value *after*, so the two are not bit-identical, `cos_sim` lands on `1 ± 1ulp`, and the distance is `±2^-23` — which is exactly the `1.1920929E-7` in the golden. Which sign it takes depends on the accumulation order of the build running the query.

That is why the framework's 1e-6 relative tolerance did not absorb it: the rows below it passed, but relative error is meaningless around zero, and `+eps` against `-eps` comes out as 2.0.

Two things confirm the diagnosis:

- **Float32 cosine is unaffected.** `test_lance_vector_search_metrics` runs the same metric over the same directional data and records a clean `0.0` self-distance, and it passed on this run. There the query literal and the stored value are bit-identical, so `cos_sim` really is 1.
- **Float16 L2 is unaffected.** `(x - x)^2` is 0 whatever the rounding; only a metric that divides by the vector norms introduces the ulp.

### Fix

The Float16 table is the one table in this suite whose data has no closed-form expected distance — Float64 records the L2 ladder `0, 16, 64, 144, 256` and UInt8 the hamming ladder `0, 1, 2, 3, 4`, both exact integers on any platform. So for Float16 the distance column was never recording a checkable value, only whatever the platform computed. Its two blocks now record `row_id, label` and the row order, which is the part that carries meaning. Float64 and UInt8 keep their distances.

The magnitude is still worth pinning — a backend that widened Float16 to Float32 before comparing, or lost the query vector's precision, would move it off one ulp — so it is now an assertion on the absolute value with a tolerance, rather than a literal whose sign a golden cannot avoid recording:

```groovy
assertTrue(Math.abs(f16SelfDistance) < 1e-5, ...)
```

I also checked the rest of `external_table_p0/lance` for the same shape: this was the only near-zero float literal in any golden there, and `f16_cosine_flat` — added in this PR, and never reached on CI because the suite aborts at the first failure — had the identical exposure. Both are fixed.

Full `external_table_p0/lance` run locally on the new head: 13/14. The one failure is `test_lance_show_index`, which needs the FE-side Lance index metadata from #66637; the FE I have running locally predates it, and CI builds the FE from this branch, which does contain it.

Automated review conclusion: approve (comment-only review; no inline findings).

Critical checkpoint conclusions:

- Goal, correctness, and proof: The change replaces the scheduler gate's single weak-CAS attempt with a linearizable exchange that always stores the requested state and returns the prior state. This removes spurious acquire and release failures while preserving every caller-visible return case. The added BE unit test directly checks the mutual-exclusion invariant under contention; it is intentionally probabilistic as a pre-fix ARM reproducer, but race-free and meaningful for the corrected contract.
- Scope and clarity: The PR is focused on the gate implementation and its targeted unit test. The explanatory comment matches the actual scheduler and revocation call graph.
- Concurrency and lifecycle: Scheduler workers, dependency requeues, and spill-revocation wrappers all serialize through the same underlying `_running` atomic. Call-site review found no unmatched/non-owner release: busy contenders only requeue, pre-execution exits release once, and the post-acquisition `Defer` releases once after normal, canceled, error, close, and finalize paths. Default sequential consistency is unchanged; no new lock order or deadlock surface is introduced.
- Parallel paths and compatibility: `RevokableTask` delegates `set_running` to the underlying `PipelineTask`, so normal execution and revocation receive the fix together. No configuration, FE/BE protocol, persisted state, storage format, rolling-upgrade, transaction, or data-visibility behavior changes.

- Tests and repository standards: The test uses joined threads and atomic bookkeeping with fixture lifetimes extending through all workers; it adds no source-file inclusion or header-hygiene issue. `git diff --check` and the available formatting/style checks are clean. Per the review-run instructions, no local build or test execution was attempted.

Review status: completed after two rounds; requesting changes for two test-lifecycle issues.

### Critical checkpoint conclusions

- **Goal and proof:** The source fix correctly breaks the no-cache `borrow()`/`read_at()` recursion. The pinned FAISS contract confirms the owning `ReadRef` keeps codes/IDs valid for each list scan. The new test reaches the intended no-cache top-N path, but its worker/deadline harness is not failure-safe.
- **Scope and clarity:** The production change is small and focused. The added asynchronous test machinery is the only unnecessary-risk area.
- **Concurrency:** `_io_mutex` continues to serialize stateful CLucene seek/read operations, and concurrent searches own independent refs. The test worker lacks the required Doris thread context, and detaching it on timeout can overlap later tests and raw singleton lifecycle.
- **Lifecycle/static state:** `OwnedReadRef` ownership and cloned `IndexInput` lifetime are correct; no cross-TU static initialization issue was introduced. The accepted lifecycle defect is the detached worker's continued access to process-global/cache state.
- **Configuration and compatibility:** No configuration, protocol, symbol, or storage-format change is introduced; rolling compatibility is unaffected.
- **Parallel paths and conditions:** Top-N and range search share the same FAISS iterator/borrow implementation, so the ownership fix applies to both. The null-cache conditional is correct, and production startup currently installs the cache unconditionally.
- **Error handling:** At the pinned FAISS revision both top-N and range iterator loops convert `std::exception` failures to `FaissException`, which Doris converts to non-OK `Status`. No new silent error path was found.
- **Tests/results:** The regression's functional setup is appropriate, but the missing thread context and unsafe detach must be fixed. The live PR reports successful compile and BE-UT checks; per the review-runner instruction, I did not run builds locally.
- **Observability:** The production cache path and its metrics are unchanged; no additional production observability is needed for this test-only reachability.
- **Transactions, persistence, data writes, and FE/BE variables:** Not applicable to this change.
- **Performance/memory:** The no-cache path performs one owning copy per current list pair and production queries retain the cache-backed tracked path. No current production performance regression was substantiated.
- **User focus:** No additional user-provided focus was supplied.

### Requested changes

1. Initialize a Doris thread context in the new raw worker.
2. Replace the in-process detach-on-timeout strategy with an isolated or bounded mechanism that cannot leak work or crash/race the shared test process.

Round 2's full and risk-focused reviewers both returned `NO_NEW_VALUABLE_FINDINGS`; all other candidates were independently dismissed with concrete code evidence or merged as duplicates.

payload.title: [fix](mtmv) skip in-flight MTMVs from Nereids MV rewrite candidates

payload.author: github-actions
payload.body:
Request changes: the current candidate check is not a complete lock-avoidance fence, and the remote running marker is not a reliable lifecycle signal.

Critical checkpoint conclusions:

- Goal and proof: The change handles the common case where an MTMV was already marked before collection, but it does not prove the stated timeout is eliminated. No test file changed, and existing tests do not exercise `hasRunningTask`, nested MTMVs, check-to-lock coordination, ambiguous remote ADD, or master failover.
- Scope and clarity: The two-file patch is small and readable, but the coordination boundary is narrower than the end-to-end mechanism it governs.
- Concurrency and locks: `runningTables` access itself is protected correctly and remains lightweight. However, the status check is not atomic with later table read-lock acquisition, and hierarchical dependencies can re-add an excluded MTMV to the same lock queue.
- Lifecycle and failover: Ordinary follower-local planning uses independent JVM locks and does not need a broadcast marker. Remote overwrite RPCs are different: the one-time, unleased marker can remain stale after an ambiguous ADD or be lost when later RPCs migrate to a promoted master.
- Configuration and compatibility: No new configuration, storage-format, function-symbol, FE-BE variable, or wire-format change is introduced. The existing remote marker RPC nevertheless needs an idempotent/recoverable operation identity before planner eligibility can rely on it.
- Parallel paths and conditions: Normal-query and DML MV-rewrite hooks share this collector. The nested-MV dependency closure is a supported parallel path that remains exposed; the pre-existing same-target admission-order behavior was reviewed and is not attributed to these changed hunks.
- Tests and results: No tests or result files were added or modified, and none were run because the review bundle explicitly forbids builds. Deterministic coordination, nested-relation, ambiguous-response, and failover tests are needed with the fix.
- Observability: The debug skip log helps for the common path, but the marker has no owner, age, or operation identity with which to diagnose stale or migrated state.
- Transactions, persistence, and data writes: The patch does not change transaction visibility or persisted table data. The identified failures occur at planner/table-lock and remote overwrite lifecycle boundaries.
- Performance: The intended removal of one-minute planner waits is incomplete, and a stale-true marker can silently disable otherwise valid MV rewrites indefinitely.
- Additional user focus: No additional user-provided focus was supplied.
- Review completion: Complete and converged in round 3. All candidates were independently validated, deduplicated, accepted, or dismissed; three inline findings remain.

payload.author: Jay-ju
payload.body:
Thanks for the thorough review. Both findings were real; fixed in the latest revision (single commit, force-pushed).

**[P1] Snapshot correctness — fixed.** The count carrier no longer serializes version 0/latest. It now pins the planned MVCC version via a new `LanceSplit.wholeDatasetCountAtVersion(uri, version, carriedRows)` factory, so a fallback scan (an old BE, or a current BE that declines the shortcut and opens the whole-dataset range in `_ensure_dataset_open`) reads exactly the snapshot the count was computed from. `wholeDatasetAtLatest` is retained only for the backend-local TVF, which is correctly latest. Added an EXPLAIN assertion (`lanceVersion=4` on the multi_frag fixture, built with three appends + three deletes) that fails if this ever regresses to latest.

**[P2] Large-count parallelism — fixed.** Since BE materializes one synthetic row per counted row, `buildCountSplits()` now shards a count `>= COUNT_WITH_PARALLEL_SPLITS` (10000, matching Iceberg) across `parallelExecInstanceNum * numBackends` fixed-version carriers, with per-carrier shares summing back to the exact total (remainder folded into the last carrier). This mirrors `IcebergScanNode.assignCountToSplits` and reuses the existing multi-split `table_level_row_count` contract, so BE needs no change. A small count stays on one carrier for backward compatibility.

Verified end to end on a real FE+BE+MinIO cluster: `count(*)` returns the logical 27 (not physical 30) for multi_frag and 12 for all_types, EXPLAIN shows `pushdown agg=COUNT (27)` with `lanceVersion=4`, and `run-regression-test test_lance_optimize_count` passes (All suites success, 0 failed).

One note on the large-count test: I kept the committed fixtures lightweight rather than adding a >=10000-row binary dataset just to cross the parallel-split threshold. The sharding is pure FE arithmetic over the existing multi-split BE contract that Iceberg/Paimon already exercise at scale, and the small-table path (single carrier) is covered by the suite. Happy to add a large fixture if you'd prefer explicit end-to-end coverage of the parallel path.

payload.author: Jay-ju
payload.body:
**Re: target branch — why this sits on branch-4.1 and not master**

A heads-up on branch choice, since I initially assumed branch-4.1 was simply "a bit ahead" of master. After checking, the whole Lance integration currently lives only on branch-4.1, not master:

- Lance was first merged to **master** via #62182, then **reverted from master** by #65303 (and the lance-c thirdparty in #65304 was likewise reverted).
- The integration was then re-established on **branch-4.1** starting from #65730, and every Lance PR since (including #66581, #66597, #66608, #66841, and this one) has targeted branch-4.1.

So branch-4.1 is intentionally ahead of master for Lance. This PR depends on that branch-4.1-only base (`LanceScanNode` / `LanceSplit` / `lance_reader`), which is why it targets branch-4.1.

Question for the maintainers: is Lance planned to be forward-ported to master? If so, I'm happy to prepare master PRs in dependency order for my changes (#66597 -> #66608 -> #66999) once the base integration (#65730 etc.) lands there. Please advise on the preferred branch strategy.

payload.body: Thanks for the update. One correctness blocker remains in the large-count path: every sharded carrier is still an unrestricted whole-dataset split. A pre-change BE ignores `table_level_row_count` and scans that whole snapshot, so rolling upgrades can count the dataset once per carrier; a current BE that declines the metadata shortcut can take the same fallback path. payload.author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer
payload.body:
## Pull request overview Fixes MySQL CDC data loss by replaying incomplete transactions after keepalive reconnects and separating heartbeat intervals. **Changes:** - Tracks and rewinds incomplete non-GTID transactions. - Configures protocol heartbeats independently from keepalive. - Adds unit/integration coverage and fixes test class loading. **Review checkpoints:** - Regular non-GTID replay is covered, but GTID file-position fallback and XA transaction boundaries remain incorrect. - Keepalive/listener lifecycle is serialized through `connectLock`; no new performance or compatibility concern found. - No new configuration or storage-format changes. ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 8 out of 8 changed files in this pull request and generated 1 comment.
Show a summary per file | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | `.licenserc.yaml` | Excludes vendored connector source. | | `BinaryLogClient.java` | Adds transaction replay state and reconnect rewind. | | `MySqlStreamingChangeEventSource.java` | Derives protocol heartbeat from progress heartbeat. | | `Constants.java` | Changes heartbeat interval to five seconds. | | `MySqlSourceReader.java` | Stops overriding keepalive interval. | | `pom.xml` | Uses compiled classes for integration tests. | | `BinaryLogClientTransactionReplayTest.java` | Tests replay-state transitions. | | `MySqlBinaryLogClientKeepAliveITCase.java` | Tests reconnect during a blocked transaction. |
Suppressed comments (2) **fs_brokers/cdc_client/src/main/java/com/github/shyiko/mysql/binlog/BinaryLogClient.java:1178** * `XA_PREPARE` is the terminal event for the XA prepare transaction group, but it does not clear the replay state here. Once `XA START` is tracked, completed XA transactions would retain an old start position and a later keepalive reconnect could replay already completed changes. Treat `XA_PREPARE` like `XID` when clearing the state. ``` if (eventType == EventType.XID || eventType == EventType.TRANSACTION_PAYLOAD) { ``` **fs_brokers/cdc_client/src/main/java/com/github/shyiko/mysql/binlog/BinaryLogClient.java:1152** * MySQL logs `XA START ...` as the begin boundary of an XA transaction. Because only the exact `BEGIN` string sets `tx`, the following after-event logic treats `XA START` as an autocommit query and clears the start marker recorded by `ANONYMOUS_GTID`. A keepalive reconnect during the XA row events can therefore still resume mid-transaction. Recognize the `XA START` prefix as a transaction start. ``` if ("BEGIN".equals(queryEventData.getSql())) { ```

Request changes. The Context-level queue-deduplication goal is clear, and the normal transfer-lock publication, dependency wakeup, final-LIMIT-block, cancellation, and TaskExecutor opt-in paths are internally coherent. However, the new default ThreadPool path still has six blocking correctness, lifecycle, error-contract, and observability issues described inline.

Critical checkpoint conclusions:
- Goal and proof: The patch implements one queued runnable per ScannerContext and atomic pending/completed/in-flight admission, but the changed unit test only exercises helpers; it never starts the rewritten scheduler or proves the worker/consumer lifecycle.
- Scope and minimality: The code change is focused on scan scheduling, but flipping both global defaults makes it a broad behavior change for internal and external scans.
- Concurrency: Operator threads and pool workers serialize pending/completed/in-flight/queued state with `transfer_lock`; scan I/O runs outside it, and no lock-order deadlock or ordinary lost-wakeup/result path was found. The no-work submission and failed-after-enqueue marker cases remain unsafe.
- Lifecycle and static state: Shared Context/task/profile ownership, normal close, cancellation, and workload-group teardown are sound; no cross-TU static initialization issue applies. Callback task attachment, exception conversion, and retained failed submissions are not sound (inline P1s).
- Configuration: No new config key is added; two existing startup-only choices change default from TaskExecutor to ThreadPool. Dynamic reload is not applicable because workload-group schedulers are constructed from the value, but both local and remote default paths must be safe before the flip.
- Compatibility: There is no wire, storage-format, or rolling-upgrade compatibility change. Queue saturation does change operator-visible error classification between scheduler implementations.
- Parallel paths and conditions: Internal/external pools and direct remote callers were traced; TaskExecutor opt-in remains intact. Shared-LIMIT EOS handling is justified and preserves the final block, but adaptive admission is missing from the parallel ThreadPool path.
- Test coverage and results: There is no real ThreadPool test for multi-block/EOS/error/LIMIT, adaptive memory, rejection, callback failure, timer accounting, or local/remote default selection. This review runner intentionally ran no builds or tests; current CI has style/formatter/license/title checks passing while BE UT, compile, and performance are pending.
- Observability: The new Context queue timer itself is consistently protected, but legacy scanner worker-wait profiles now include consumer backpressure, and raw rejection loses the established scan-pool classification/context.
- Transactions, persistence, data writes, and FE-BE variables: Not applicable; the patch changes read scheduling only and introduces no persisted state, write transaction, or cross-layer variable.

Request changes — capped/incomplete after the third review round.

I found five additional distinct issues on the current head:

- P1: default dry-run modeled waits exceed brpc `LatencyRecorder`'s integer input range within seconds under sustained overload, causing clamped/corrupt metrics and per-request WARNING amplification before Doris's log gates.
- P1: the table strict limiter's unslept dry-run deadline can overflow its signed nanosecond `steady_clock` representation while dry-run remains enabled.
- P1: tick-thread startup failure is logged and ignored, leaving the default-on upgrade path active without its only downgrade/recovery driver.
- P1: the host token bucket's unslept dry-run debt eventually makes its `double`-to-`int64_t` wait conversion undefined while dry-run remains enabled.
- P2: default-on first touches allocate/construct bvars and perform the first increment while holding the registry-wide exclusive lock, serializing unrelated tables and RPC types.

Previously raised blockers also remain: [dry-run debt entering enforcement](https://github.com/apache/doris/pull/66977#discussion_r3820229232), [default dry-run overriding configured enforcement](https://github.com/apache/doris/pull/66977#discussion_r3820229238), [rollback double-booking enforced reservations](https://github.com/apache/doris/pull/66977#discussion_r3820229241), [cleanup-worker startup failure](https://github.com/apache/doris/pull/66977#discussion_r3852926004), [uncoupled throttle-state retention](https://github.com/apache/doris/pull/66977#discussion_r3852926024), and [mutable-cooldown elapsed-time loss](https://github.com/apache/doris/pull/66977#discussion_r3852926029). Current head does address the earlier deferred-QPS-read, coordinator-counter, floor-history, and eviction-side destruction comments.

Checkpoint conclusions:

- Goal and correctness: the ordinary dry-run path observes without sleeping, but the default-on feature is not safe across sustained overload, mode transitions, worker failure, or rollback timelines.
- Scope, compatibility, and configuration: the patch is localized and introduces no wire/storage/schema/FE-BE protocol change. The new default behavior is nevertheless incompatible with deployments that already enabled enforcement, and both mode pairs share mutable enforcement state without transition callbacks.
- Concurrency, lifecycle, and performance: no additional deadlock, lock-order inversion, UAF, ownership cycle, or unsafe destruction order was found. The accepted tick-driver failure, create-side global critical section, cleanup failure, and uncoupled per-table state remain material.
- Parallel paths, errors, and retries: all 22 host slots and five table mappings were accounted for; each generic retry attempt limits once, calls once, records once, then handles MS_BUSY. The direct GETROWSET retry loop correctly remains host-only. Status propagation is otherwise unchanged.
- Tests and results: this was a source-only review; builds/tests were prohibited by the review prompt. The changed unit tests cover short happy paths, cleanup survival, resets, floor no-ops, logging admission, and ordinary timing, but miss recorder/numeric boundaries, both injected worker-start failures, enforcement sleepers during rollback, sustained cardinality/progress, mode compatibility, and discarded elapsed time before a cooldown increase. payload.body:
Automated review status: complete and converged after three rounds. Requesting changes for three P1 correctness issues.

Findings

1. The FE materialization rule moves sensitive Map inputs from Join candidate-pair scope into a child-row Project, changing outer-join error behavior and volatile evaluation frequency.
2. The same rule moves computed Maps out of selector-controlled IF/CASE branches, defeating supported short-circuit execution.
3. The BE eight-batch direct path bypasses the variable-width lambda safety ceiling and can turn a bounded query into a multi-gigabyte ColumnString overflow.

Checkpoint conclusions

- Goal and scope: the advertised Map lambda wrappers, constructors, tuple syntax, recursive NULL-type handling, and FE-to-BE lowerings are present. The scalar wrappers and registrations are localized; the 786-line late materialization rule and the unrelated ArrayMap batching expansion are the principal risk surfaces.
- Planner semantics and parallel paths: Project, OneRowRelation, Filter, Having, normalized Aggregate, Generate, Join metadata, nested lambda ExprIds, marker translation, and second-pass stability were reviewed. Outside the two inline evaluation-domain failures, no additional owner or parallel path defect survived.
- Types, nullability, compatibility, and physical symbols: lambda arity, Map-key legality, nullable Maps/predicates, nested NULL_TYPE merging, last-win semantics, and the names `map_from_arrays`, `%map_from_arrays_unique%`, `map_filter`, and `map_from_entries` align across FE and BE. No serialized format or existing function signature changes.
- Runtime correctness and ownership: constant/nullable wrappers, offsets, selected rows, invalid entries, duplicate keys, COW detachment, and Status propagation were checked. Those paths remain sound outside the accepted lambda budget issue.
- Performance and memory: the direct-path multiplier is a correctness failure as well as an allocation regression; no other distinct performance defect survived review.
- Concurrency, lifecycle, configuration, persistence, transactions, writes, and observability: no new applicable mechanism is introduced.
- Tests: the changed unit and regression sources broadly cover ordinary, null, constant, duplicate, empty, nested, aggregate, Join, Generate, and selected-row behavior, but omit the three accepted boundaries. Per the automated-review contract, I did not run builds or tests; current style, license, formatting, and secret checks pass, while build/test jobs are skipped.
- User focus: no additional focus was supplied.

No pre-existing live review thread or comment duplicated these findings.

Finding

- Native-table access-path pruning can lose Map values used only inside a nested Lambda and substitute default/null values; one inline comment is attached.
- The existing [P1 variable-width Lambda budget thread](https://github.com/apache/doris/pull/66968#discussion_r3828974256) remains applicable and was not duplicated.

Critical checkpoint conclusions

- Goal and proof: the PR adds Map Lambda functions, Map constructors/filtering, tuple Lambda syntax, and FE-to-BE lowering. Registrations and ordinary semantics align, and unit/regression sources cover null, empty, duplicate, constant, computed, nondeterministic, nested, aggregate, Join, and Generate cases; the accepted native stored-column boundary is not covered.
- Scope and focus: the implementation is cohesive for the advertised feature and reuses ArrayMap/MapEntries/Map primitives. No additional user focus was supplied.
- Concurrency: execution uses query-local expression/column state; no new shared mutable state, locks, lock ordering, or thread-safety mechanism is introduced.
- Lifecycle/static initialization: Lambda frames use scoped guards and ColumnMap sharing uses COW; no non-intuitive release path, circular ownership, or cross-TU static initialization dependency was found.
- Configuration: no configuration item or dynamic-update path is added.
- Compatibility: FE wrapper names, arities, return/nullability types, and internal physical symbols match BE registration. No storage format, persisted metadata, or protocol variable changes are introduced; the new function symbols are additive.
- Parallel paths: public Map functions, internal unique/filtered constructors, legacy two-argument `map_filter`, constant folding, computed inputs, nested Lambdas, and native/external scan paths were checked. The native scan divergence is the attached finding.
- Conditional checks: const broadcasting, top-level null Maps/arrays, hidden null-row payloads, mismatched offsets, nullable predicates, and last-win deduplication checks have explicit failure/skip behavior and targeted tests. No separate conditional-check defect survived.
- Test coverage: BE unit tests and FE/regression tests are broad, including negative cases, but need a stored native-table test where the outer Map Lambda retains the key and reads the value only inside an inner Lambda.
- Test results: the committed `.out` results match the asserted ordinary semantics. Per the review-run contract, I did not run builds or tests.
- Observability: these are scalar analysis/execution paths; existing AnalysisException/Status failures are sufficient, and no new log or metric is required.
- Transactions/persistence: no transaction, EditLog, master-failover, or persistent-state path is changed.
- Data writes/crashes: the feature is query-time only and does not modify stored data. COW detachment and Status propagation are sound outside the accepted read-pruning correctness issue.
- FE-BE variables: no new session/protocol variable is transmitted. FE and BE independently computed types/names were checked and agree.
- Performance: zero-copy/COW paths are reasonable, but the existing live byte-budget P1 remains unresolved; no distinct additional CPU/memory issue survived duplicate fencing.
- Other issues: the scalar-subquery tuple-parser candidate was rejected because the semantic predicate only gates, rather than forces, its alternative. No other unresolved candidate remains.

Empty/all-literal arrays, scalar array(...), nested/mixed/null arrays, and function-binding paths were checked. No storage, serialization, public protocol, or rolling-upgrade change is involved.

Per the review environment instruction, no build or tests were run. Current applicable CI style/security checks pass; several unrelated jobs are skipped and the code-review check is pending.
